opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't think of it as a "paradigm update." I was an undergraduate at Tsinghua, working with Professor Wang Zhong, and we were just trying to understand something that looked like a puzzle.

The background is that in topological physics there's a very beautiful, very well-established idea called bulk-boundary correspondence. You compute a topological invariant from the bulk, using the band structure with periodic boundary conditions, and that tells you how many protected edge states you'll see when you cut the system open. It's almost a dogma. Everyone believed it, and for Hermitian systems it really works.

Then people started looking at non-Hermitian systems, systems with gain and loss, or open systems coupled to an environment. When you numerically compared the periodic spectrum with the open-boundary spectrum, they just didn't match. Not slightly off, but completely different. People tried to patch the existing framework, defining new invariants and arguing about which one was "correct."

What we realized was that the problem wasn't the invariant. It was a hidden assumption underneath everything: that the bulk eigenstates are Bloch waves, extended plane waves spread across the system. In these non-Hermitian systems that's simply false. When you open the boundary, essentially all the eigenstates pile up at one edge. We called this the non-Hermitian skin effect. Once you see that, the whole puzzle reorganizes itself. You can't use the ordinary Brillouin zone anymore. You need a generalized one, where the momentum becomes complex, and if you compute the topology on that object, bulk-boundary correspondence is restored.

So looking back, the reason I'd call it a paradigm update rather than just a new result is that it wasn't about adding a new term to an existing theory. It was about noticing that a concept everyone used without thinking, Bloch's theorem and the Brillouin zone, had quietly stopped being valid. Many of the confusions at the time came from people asking good questions inside a framework that no longer applied.

That experience stayed with me. When a field is stuck and everyone is debating details, it's often worth stepping back and asking which basic assumption we all take for granted might be wrong. Most of the time the answer is "none of them." But occasionally one is, and then things that looked very complicated become surprisingly simple. I think that habit of mind was probably the most valuable thing I took from physics, more than any specific result.

r001.rationale: It describes the periodic-boundary and open-boundary spectra as completely different in the context of the bulk-boundary correspondence problem.

r002.rationale: It says the assumed extended Bloch-wave description of bulk eigenstates is false in these non-Hermitian systems.

r003.rationale: It states that essentially all eigenstates pile up at one edge when the boundary is opened.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it didn't feel like a paradigm update at the start. It felt like a bug.

This was around 2017, when I was a PhD student with Zhong Wang at Tsinghua. We were looking at a very simple non-Hermitian lattice model, basically the SSH chain with an asymmetry in the hopping, so electrons find it easier to hop to the right than to the left. The standard playbook in topological physics is that you compute the band structure for an infinite periodic system, you get a topological invariant from the bulk, and that number tells you how many edge states you'll see when you cut the system open. Bulk-boundary correspondence. It's the thing everyone trusts.

So we did the bulk calculation, we did the numerics on a finite open chain, and they disagreed. Not slightly. The edge states appeared at the wrong parameters. The spectrum with open boundaries looked nothing like the spectrum with periodic boundaries. My first reaction was that I had made a mistake in the code. I rewrote it. Same result.

The moment things turned was when we actually plotted the eigenstates instead of just the eigenvalues. In a Hermitian system, bulk states are extended, they spread over the whole chain like waves. Here, essentially every single eigenstate was crammed up against one end of the chain. Not just a few edge modes. All of them. Thousands of states, all piled up at the boundary. We later called this the non-Hermitian skin effect, because the "bulk" of the system had effectively moved to its skin.

Once you see that picture, you realize the problem isn't the model. The problem is the assumption. Bloch's theorem says a periodic system has plane-wave eigenstates with a real wavevector k. That is baked into how we define bands, Brillouin zones, everything. But if every state is exponentially localized at one end, the states are not plane waves anymore. They're plane waves with an exponential envelope, which means k has picked up an imaginary part. The wavevector has become complex.

So the fix was to let k be complex and ask: for an open chain, which complex values of k are actually allowed? That gives you a curve in the complex plane instead of a circle, which we called the generalized Brillouin zone. If you compute your topological invariant on that curve instead of the usual one, bulk-boundary correspondence is restored. The prediction and the numerics finally agree.

What made me think of it as a paradigm shift rather than just a technical patch was realizing how much had silently depended on the old assumption. Band theory is nearly a century old. Its central object, the Brillouin zone, was being treated as given even in a regime where its foundations had quietly collapsed. Non-Hermitian physics had been studied for years at that point, in optics, in open quantum systems, and people had noticed strange things about boundary sensitivity, but mostly treated them as anomalies. The reframing was: these aren't anomalies, the periodic-boundary description is simply the wrong starting point. You need non-Bloch band theory.

I think that's often how these things go. You're not looking for a new framework. You're trying to get two plots to match. And then at some point you notice that the only way to make them match is to give up something you were taught never to question.

r001.rationale: It says the bulk calculation and finite open-chain numerics disagreed, and that open- and periodic-boundary spectra looked very different.

r002.rationale: It explains that eigenstates are not ordinary plane waves and that the usual Bloch description breaks down, requiring complex wavevectors.

r003.rationale: It states that essentially every eigenstate was crammed against one end of the chain, describing all states accumulating at a boundary.

astra-6.text:
For me, it became a paradigm update when I realized that we weren’t simply adding a small correction to the usual picture. We were having to reconsider some of the assumptions behind that picture.

In a Hermitian system, we’re accustomed to using the properties of an infinite, periodic bulk to understand what happens at a boundary. But in a non-Hermitian system, changing the boundary conditions can change the behavior of an extensive number of states. States that we would ordinarily think of as bulk states can accumulate near an edge. That means the boundary is doing something much more consequential than merely terminating the material.

The conceptual question then becomes: what is the right description of the bulk? If we keep applying the familiar framework without examining its assumptions, the predictions can seem contradictory. Once we change the framework, those contradictions become understandable.

That’s the sense in which I understand a paradigm update. It isn’t that the old theory becomes wrong. It’s that we recognize the conditions under which it works, and discover that a broader class of systems requires a different starting point.

r001.rationale: The response says boundary conditions can change many states’ behavior and that familiar predictions can seem contradictory, but it does not identify a mismatch between topological results under periodic and open boundary conditions.

r002.rationale: It questions using the properties of an infinite periodic bulk, but does not state that the Bloch-wave description of eigenstates breaks down in non-Hermitian systems.

r003.rationale: It says states can accumulate near an edge, without saying that all energy eigenstates may accumulate at the same boundary.

sol-6.1.text:
I came to see it that way because we ran into something that looked, at first, like a fairly technical problem: how do you describe the topology of a non-Hermitian system? But the difficulty turned out to involve a basic assumption about how we understand a bulk material.

Usually, we study a periodic system, calculate its energy bands, and use those bands to predict what happens when we introduce a boundary. In the non-Hermitian setting, that connection can break down. With open boundaries, even the bulk eigenstates can accumulate near an edge—the non-Hermitian skin effect. So the boundary is no longer just a small correction to an otherwise unchanged bulk.

That was the conceptual shift for me. We couldn’t simply take the familiar framework and allow the energies to become complex. We had to reconsider how bulk states are described and how bulk properties predict boundary behavior. The non-Bloch description was a way to rebuild that connection.

So by a paradigm update, I mean that the questions remain recognizable, but some of the assumptions behind our usual answers have to change. What initially seems like an exception can point toward a broader framework.

r001.rationale: The response says the usual connection between periodic bands and boundary behavior can break down, but does not clearly identify a mismatch between topological results under periodic and open boundary conditions.

r002.rationale: It says the familiar framework must be reconsidered, but does not state that the Bloch-wave description used for Hermitian systems can break down.

r003.rationale: It says bulk eigenstates can accumulate near an edge, but does not say that all energy eigenstates may accumulate at the same boundary.
